Magnetic Fields and Forces on Moving Cha: A magnetic field B, measured in teslas (T), is created by magnets and moving charges. Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole. A charge q moving with velocity v in a field experiences a force F = q v B sin(theta), perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule). The force does no work, so it changes the direction but not the speed. A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field moves in a circle of radius r = m v / (q B) and period T = 2 pi m / (q B). The Earth has a magnetic field of about 5 x 10^-5 T. Applications include mass spectrometers, cyclotrons and cathode-ray tubes.
Magnetic Force on Currents and Magnetic: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force F = I L B sin(theta), where L is the length of wire in the field. Two parallel wires attract if their currents are in the same direction and repel if opposite; this defines the ampere. A current produces its own magnetic field. A long straight wire gives B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), with mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A; the field lines form circles around the wire (right-hand grip rule). A circular loop of radius R gives B = mu_0 I / (2 R) at its center, and a long solenoid with n turns per meter has a uniform field B = mu_0 n I inside. Electromagnets and motors use these effects.
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's: A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf. The magnetic flux is Phi = B A cos(theta), in webers (Wb = T m^2). Faraday's law gives the induced emf: emf = -N delta Phi / delta t for a coil of N turns. Lenz's law (the minus sign) says the induced current opposes the change in flux that produced it. For a rod of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to a field, the emf is emf = B L v. A generator turns a coil in a magnetic field and produces an alternating emf, emf = N B A omega sin(omega t). Induction is also used in transformers, induction cooktops and metal detectors.
Inductance, Transformers and AC: A changing current in a coil induces an emf in the coil itself: emf = -L delta I / delta t, where L is the inductance in henries. The energy stored in an inductor is 1/2 L I^2. A transformer changes an alternating voltage: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p, and for an ideal transformer V_p I_p = V_s I_s. A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary. Alternating current varies sinusoidally; the rms values are V_rms = V_peak / sqrt(2) and I_rms = I_peak / sqrt(2), and the average power is P = I_rms V_rms. Mains of 230 V rms have a peak of about 325 V. Transformers cannot work with direct current.
Magnetic Materials, Motors and Applicati: Materials respond to magnetic fields in different ways. Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) are strongly attracted because their atoms form magnetic domains that line up in an external field; they can be permanently magnetized and lose their magnetism above the Curie temperature. Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted and diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled. An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core, which multiplies the field. A DC motor uses the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, F = I L B, with a split-ring commutator to keep the torque in one direction; the torque on a coil is tau = N I A B sin(theta). A generator is the reverse process. A mass spectrometer uses r = m v / (q B) to separate ions by mass, and the Hall effect uses the sideways force on moving charges to measure fields.
